# Research: Fix Multi-Level CSV Header Skip Rule

## How `...N` names end up in CSV files

**Decision**: The `...N` names (matching `^\\.\\.\\.\\d+$`) are baked into the CSV text at export time — they are not generated by `read.delim` at read time.

**Rationale**: `readxl::read_excel()` generates `...1`, `...2`, … as placeholder names for empty or merged header cells when reading Excel files. When a user exports such an xlsx to CSV, those placeholder names are written literally as column headers. When `read.delim` later reads that CSV with `check.names = FALSE`, it sees `...1` as a real column name value.

**Implication**: The fix must work with the already-read `df` — coercing its early rows to character to find the sub-header, then renaming in-memory. A second file read is unnecessary.

---

## Why the current 50% threshold produces false positives

**Decision**: The threshold correctly detects the symptom (many `...N` names) but conflates two distinct root causes.

**Root cause A — Fully placeholder row 1, real labels on row 2+**: Files 2 (`Fitting_Foglio1.csv`), 3 (`MTTDATA_Raw Data.csv`), and 5 (`Avreaged raw data_Sheet1.csv`). Row 1 is almost entirely `...N` (75–87%). The actual raw variable names live on row 2 (or row 3 for file 5). These need sub-header detection (Branch 1).

**Root cause B — Partial-label row 1, data on row 2**: File 1 (`Experiment 3_Summary_MTT_Foglio1.csv`). Row 1 has names like `Passato...3`, `Futuro...6` — partially informative. 60% are pure `...N`. There is no sub-header row (row 2 is numeric participant data). This file is processed as-is with its partial names (Branch 2).

---

## Column naming strategy: why sub-header name becomes `column_name`

**Decision**: The resolved sub-header name (row 2+) becomes `column_name` in `columns.csv`. The row-1 condition/group label is captured separately in `col_header_group`. The original `...N` placeholder is not persisted.

**Rationale — codebook matching**: Codebooks describe raw variable names as they appear in the data (e.g., `PAST_Mortgage`, `BLOCK1`, `Subject`). These correspond exactly to the sub-header row values. If `column_name` holds the sub-header value, `match_column_labels()` in `helper.R` works without any modification — `normalize_varname(column_name)` produces a matchable string directly.

If instead `column_name` held the original `...N` value, `match_column_labels()` would produce `normalize_varname("...3") = "...3"` — which will never match any codebook variable. This would require changes to `helper.R` and `2_codebook_label.R` to use a secondary resolved-name field, adding complexity with no benefit.

**Rationale — future pivot**: These files are wide-format experimental data where conditions (SHAM/BETA/ALPHA, RB_TASK/II_TASK) are encoded as column spans in row 1. A future wide→long pivot needs to know which columns belong to the same condition group. This information lives in the row-1 span labels, not in the sub-header variable names. Storing it in `col_header_group` (forward-filled across the span) provides a clean pivot key without embedding it in `column_name` or requiring compound names like `SHAM.PAST_Mortgage`.

**Why not compound names** (e.g., `SHAM.PAST_Mortgage`): Compound names would require prefix-stripping in `match_column_labels()` for codebook matching to work. The codebook has `PAST_Mortgage`, not `SHAM.PAST_Mortgage`. Keeping the raw variable name in `column_name` and the group label separate avoids this entirely.

**Why not preserve `...N` as a separate field**: The `...N` placeholder carries no information useful to codebook matching, future pivoting, or any other downstream step. It is an Excel export artifact — an absence of a name, not a name in itself. Persisting it would add schema noise without value.

---

## `col_header_group` forward-fill algorithm

**Decision**: Extract the non-`...N` prefix from each row-1 column name, then forward-fill across the span of pure-`...N` columns that follow.

**Algorithm**: Strip `...\d+` suffix from each `names(df)` value. Non-empty results are group labels; empty results (`...N` → `""`) become NA. Iterate left to right: when a non-NA label is encountered, record it as `last_grp` and assign it to all subsequent NA positions until the next non-NA label.

**Example** — `MTTDATA_Raw Data.csv` row-1 names:

```
...1        → NA    → NA   (no group yet)
...2        → NA    → NA
SHAM...3    → SHAM  → SHAM
...4 – ...8 → NA    → SHAM (filled)
BETA...9    → BETA  → BETA
...10-...14 → NA    → BETA (filled)
ALPHA...15  → ALPHA → ALPHA
```

Columns before the first named group label (e.g., subject index col 1 and 2) retain `NA` — they are not part of any condition span.

---

## Sub-header detection algorithm

**Decision**: Scan rows 1 through `MULTILEVEL_HEADER_LOOKAHEAD` (default 3) of the already-read `df`. A row qualifies as a better sub-header if its `...N` fraction is strictly lower than the current header's fraction AND it contains at least one non-empty, non-NA, non-`...N` value.

Use the **first qualifying row** — not the one with the fewest `...N` values. First qualifying is simpler and correct for all known cases.

**NA cells in the sub-header**: Fall back to the original `...N` name from row 1. This preserves column uniqueness and is preferable to auto-generating names.

**Duplicate column names after resolution**: Apply `make.unique()` to the resolved name vector. This handles cases where the same variable name appears under multiple condition spans (e.g., `PAST_Mortgage` under SHAM, BETA, ALPHA) — producing `PAST_Mortgage`, `PAST_Mortgage.1`, `PAST_Mortgage.2`. The `col_header_group` field disambiguates these for downstream processing.

---

## File 5: 3-level header — which row is used

**Decision**: For `Avreaged raw data_Sheet1.csv` (3-level header), the algorithm picks row 2 as the sub-header (first qualifying row), not row 3.

- Row 1: `...N`-heavy (87%), group labels: `RB_TASK`, `II_TASK`, `Discrimination task`
- Row 2: `SUBJECT`, `LEARNING`, `TEST` — qualifies at depth 1
- Row 3: `Subject`, `GROUP`, `BLOCK1`…`BLOCK8` — also qualifies but not reached

Row 2 values (`SUBJECT`, `LEARNING`, `TEST`) are valid variable labels for codebook matching purposes. Row 3 (`BLOCK1`–`BLOCK8`) would be more granular but introduces more duplicate names. Using the first qualifying row is consistent and simpler.

---

## Scope: files changed

**Decision**: Only `0_index.R` and `output-schemas.md` change.

- `read_data_head()` in `helper.R` — unchanged (generic reader; multi-level logic belongs in extraction stage)
- `match_column_labels()` in `helper.R` — unchanged (works directly on `column_name`, which is now the resolved sub-header value)
- `2_codebook_label.R` — unchanged (`column_name` in `columns.csv` is already the right key; no new field needs propagating to `labels.csv`)
- `output-schemas.md` — add `col_header_group` column to `columns.csv` schema table

---

## New constant: `MULTILEVEL_HEADER_LOOKAHEAD`

**Decision**: Add `MULTILEVEL_HEADER_LOOKAHEAD <- 3L` to the constants block in `0_index.R`.

**Default value 3**: Covers all known real-world cases (max depth observed: 3 header rows in `Avreaged raw data_Sheet1.csv`).
